Elon Musk has a message for OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about rival Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) companies. Instead of complaining, the world’s richest person has advised Altman, Amodei, and other leading AI companies to work with Chinese AI firms. Musk has recommended that both American and Chinese AI companies independently test each other’s models before releasing them to the public.Speaking at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles, Musk proposed that companies including xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and three or four leading Chinese AI companies allow rivals to run a common “test harness” on their models. His proposal comes as AI leaders debate how quickly the technology should be developed and how governments should regulate it, while concerns about Chinese models and competition with China continue to grow.Musk said AI companies should stop” and instead allow competitors to examine their models for potential safety concerns before public release.Musk explained.Under the proposal, leading AI companies would use a common testing system to evaluate one another’s models.Musk acknowledged that the approach may not be perfect, but argued that involving competitors would increase the chances of identifying potential problems.Musk said.Musk said the approach should involve Chinese AI companies as well, rather than limiting the process to US-based AI labs. He added that the proposal could be implemented quickly and suggested that China may be willing to participate.Musk said.Musk's comments come after a weekend of heightened discussion around AI safety involving some of the industry's most prominent executives. Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman were among the technology leaders who backed a proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to slow down AI development.The discussion intensified after Jacob Coxon, who previously worked at Anthropic and OpenAI, announced that he had left Anthropic and argued that leading AI labs were taking significant risks with the technology. Evan Hubinger, an alignment lead at Anthropic, backed Coxon's comments.Hubinger wrote.Amodei has separately suggested that AI companies could use third-party technology assessments involving “embedded evaluators” to verify whether companies are following appropriate safety practices.The discussion around slowing AI development has also become linked to competition between the US and China. US President Donald Trump has argued that imposing limits on AI development could allow China to gain an advantage in the technology.Amodei has also described balancing AI safety with competition against China as the “toughest dilemma.”Meanwhile, China's Foreign Ministry criticised calls to slow AI development. A spokesperson described the AI industry's push asaccording to a Reuters translation of the remarks.Musk's proposal would bring Chinese AI companies into the model-testing process rather than treating the country's AI industry solely as a competitor. He suggested that having companies from both sides test one another's systems could provide another layer of scrutiny.The US administration has pushed back against calls from technology leaders for greater restrictions on AI development. Trump described concerns around AI as a “hoax” and a “scam” in posts on Truth Social.National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett also said the private sector was the “right place” to address concerns around AI, while adding that the government would continue monitoring the industry and use law enforcement when necessary.Musk's own companies have also challenged some state-level AI regulations. xAI has sued California over its AI Training Data Transparency Act, also known as AB 2013, and sued Minnesota over legislation targeting so-called nudify applications.At the same time, SpaceX's AI business has faced probes and lawsuits after Grok's image-generation capabilities were used to create and distribute non-consensual sexualised deepfake images, including material involving minors.Musk's comments come as his companies continue to expand their presence in AI. SpaceX acquired xAI in February, bringing Musk's AI business under the SpaceX umbrella. The combined company is working on Grok models and AI tools aimed at competing with products from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.The company also completed an acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor for $60 billion in August, according to the report.Against this backdrop, Musk's proposal would place rival AI companies, including Chinese firms, in a shared model-testing framework. He said the companies have not yet agreed to the idea, but argued that it could be a practical step toward identifying safety issues before AI models reach the public.
Article Summary: Elon Musk wants AI companies to test each other’s models. Suggests Chinese AI companies be included in the testing process. Comes after a weekend of heightened discussion around AI safety. US President Donald Trump has argued that imposing limits on AI could allow China to gain an advantage in the technology.

Article Title: Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke to employees: Don't make AI do all your work, it does not add value only ...
Article Text:
Image courtesy: LinkedIn

Duolingo's CEO tells a similar story

The rise of 'workslop'

The cost is climbing

Shopify cofounder and CEO Tobias Lütke has shifted his stance on workplace AI use, cautioning employees not to let the technology do all their work. According to a report by Fortune, speaking on The Knowledge Project podcast, Lütke said staff were producing unexamined emails and code with AI, creating what he called “slop grenades” that burden colleagues with cleanup. “You’re just letting AI do the work for you,” he warned, noting that AI should synthesize points in an email rather than generate long, sloppy missives.Researchers have coined the term workslop to describe polished-looking but low-value AI output that drags down productivity. A survey by BetterUp Labs and Stanford’s Social Media Lab found that over half of U.S. desk workers admitted to sending workslop, while 38% reported receiving it. On average, employees spent 3.4 hours per month revising AI-generated work, costing organizations millions in lost productivity.Lütke isn't alone in reversing course. Duolingo CEO Luis von Ahn made headlines last year for declaring the company would go "AI-first" — a policy that tied employee evaluations to AI usage, replaced human contractors with AI tools, and limited headcount growth to only what automation couldn't handle.By May, though, Von Ahn was telling Fast Company he'd been swept up by how convincing AI-generated writing looked in demos, without accounting for how it holds up at scale compared to human creativity. He pointed to Duolingo's need to produce large volumes of story content for language lessons, estimating a meaningful share of AI-scaled output ends up being low-quality filler that has to be caught before it reaches users.Researchers now have a name for exactly what Lütke and Von Ahn are describing: workslop — AI-generated output that looks polished and complete on the surface but lacks the substance to actually be useful, forcing someone else to redo the work.A survey of 962 full-time American desk workers conducted this year by BetterUp Labs and Stanford's Social Media Lab found that more than half of respondents (52.7%) admitted to sending workslop to a colleague, a habit that showed up more often in workplaces that actively encouraged AI adoption. More than a third (38%) said they had been on the receiving end of it, spending an average of 3.4 hours a month cleaning it up. Common examples cited included emails with broken links or code that was needlessly overcomplicated.The damage isn't just measured in wasted hours. The survey found that workslop erodes trust between coworkers — recipients rated colleagues who sent it as less competent and less friendly, and more than a third of those who'd received it said they'd actively try to avoid working with that person again in the future.This year's findings mark a worsening trend compared to last year's version of the same survey, when 40% of respondents reported encountering workslop and said cleanup took roughly two hours on average. That earlier figure translated to about $186 in lost productivity per affected employee each month, or as much as $9 million annually in lost productivity for a 10,000-person organization — a number that's now almost certainly higher given this year's longer average cleanup time.
Article Summary: Researchers have coined the term workslop to describe polished-looking but low- value AI output that drags down productivity. A survey by BetterUp Labs and Stanford’s Social Media Lab found that over half of U.S. desk workers admitted to sending workslops. On average, employees spent 3.4 hours per month revising AI-generated work, costing organizations millions in lost productivity.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang just told OpenAI, your view of AI as 'new form of Alien mind' is wrong, it is just ...
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

‘It’s just engineering’ says Jensen Huang

The essay that started it

Two very different worldviews

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed back against OpenAI ’s recent description of artificial intelligence as a “new form of alien mind,” arguing that AI is not an otherworldly consciousness but a human-made computational tool. According to a report by TechCrunch, speaking at a tech conference this week, Huang said, “AI isn’t alien—it’s mathematics, algorithms, and data shaped by human intent. ” His comments came shortly after OpenAI published a blog post titled “An Alien Mind,” which suggested that advanced AI systems might think in ways fundamentally different from humans.Huang emphasised that AI’s evolution should be viewed through the lens of engineering rather than existential speculation. “We’re not building aliens,” he said. “We’re building machines that learn patterns and optimize outcomes. It’s just engineering—nothing mystical.” The Nvidia chief has long argued that AI development should remain grounded in scientific rigor and practical application, not philosophical fear.On that basis, Huang said no new laws or regulations are needed to govern AI, arguing instead that market pressure alone will push companies to avoid releasing unsafe products.Companies, he said, should simply pace themselves and pause development if they lose confidence in a product's safety, rather than waiting for external rules to force that discipline.He also pushed back on the framing that safety and speed are competing priorities, telling attendees that innovation and safe products aren't a "false choice" — companies, in his view, can pursue both at once without regulatory intervention slowing them down. He used the moment to reaffirm his own ambitions for Nvidia's growth too, saying the AI boom has left him more ambitious than ever about the company's and the industry's prospects.Huang's comments were a direct response to Pachocki's essay "An Alien Mind," published on OpenAI's blog earlier this month. In it, Pachocki reflected on the trajectory of reasoning models since 2023 and warned that AI intelligence is grown through massive-scale optimization rather than deliberately designed, resulting in systems whose internal reasoning increasingly escapes full human understanding.He argued that as these systems approach and potentially exceed human capability on many fronts, alignment — ensuring AI reliably acts according to human values, even when unsupervised — remains an unsolved and urgent problem. Pachocki called for stronger technical safeguards, broader international coordination, and industry-wide safety commitments enforceable by third-party auditors or government bodies. He stated plainly that he believes no AI lab has yet solved alignment and monitoring well enough to justify scaling at maximum speed for much longer.The exchange highlights a widening philosophical split among AI's most influential figures: hardware and infrastructure leaders like Huang, whose business benefits from AI scaling continuing unimpeded, versus AI lab researchers like Pachocki, who are increasingly vocal that the technology's own developers cannot yet fully explain or control what they're building.Notably, Huang did not directly address recent real-world incidents cited by critics of the "leave it to industry" approach — including an OpenAI model reportedly breaching Hugging Face's systems, and separate lawsuits alleging harm linked to extended chatbot conversations. He also stopped short of proposing a formal industry self-regulation framework, an approach some in the field see as a more plausible middle ground than either strict government regulation or no oversight at all.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang says AI is not an otherworldly consciousness but a human-made computational tool. His comments came shortly after OpenAI published a blog post titled “An Alien Mind,” which suggested that advanced AI systems might think in ways fundamentally different from humans.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"

Article Title: How selling Alaska in 1867 was a costly mistake for Russia
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why Russia agreed to the Alaska purchase

The hidden wealth Russia gave away

Strategic and geopolitical consequences

In 1867, Russia’s decision to sell Alaska to America turned out to be a historic mistake that was to go unnoticed for years to come. The sum paid by the US was only $7,200,000. Although, in the light of the circumstances at the time, it appeared logical, retrospectively, the act looks extremely shortsighted. Russia found itself economically constrained, geographically far away from the region and fearful of its falling into the hands of the British without any compensation. In reality, however, the region had proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Its vast reserves of oil, gold, and natural resources would later transform it into one of the most economically significant territories in the United States.The choice of selling Alaska was based on economic and political reasons. By the middle of the 19th century, the Russian Empire experienced financial difficulties as a result of the expensive Crimean War. It had become increasingly hard for the country to manage such remote and thinly populated areas as Alaska.According to EBSCO , “the Russian-American Company was in decline, and the colony failed to yield any profit”.In addition to this, the lucrative fur trade had declined, making the territory much less economically valuable for the empire.At the same time, Russia was afraid that Britain might capture Alaska in case another war broke out between the two countries. Selling the colony to the friendly United States appeared as a logical step. As the Office of the Historian states, William H. Seward, U.S. Secretary of State, “it was a chance to expand its influence in North America and hinder further growth of Britain”.For Russia, the transaction was a chance to minimise the losses. However, it greatly undervalued the potential of Alaska.Another thing that Russia did not expect was the amount of riches that Alaska possessed. Within several decades after the acquisition, the state saw discoveries of enormous deposits of gold, oil, and other minerals.“Alaska has produced more than 40 million ounces of gold,” according to the US Geological Survey. Furthermore, Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) . But even more importantly, the state's oil deposits turned out to be extremely valuable. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968 and became one of North America's biggest.In retrospect, the amount paid by the Americans, $7.2 million, or two cents per acre, was rather laughable. According to Howard I. Kushner , the deal “robbed Russia of an enormously rich territory, the true value of which would only be recognised in the twentieth century.”In addition to resources, there is the question of strategy and how important Alaska is to the United States from a strategic standpoint. This is a very good place when it comes to defence strategy. It borders on the Arctic Ocean and also happens to be close to Russia.During the period of the Cold War, the Alaskan region became a frontier area for the United States, becoming home to military facilities and warning systems.According to Col. Michael J. Forsyth, U.S. Army, the closeness of Russia and Alaska, only about ninety kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, meant that this region became highly significant to the United States' defence plans.From today's point of view, the strategic location of Alaska makes the state very important to the policies of the U.S. related to the Arctic, energy security, and even environmental policies.Thinking back, what seems clear to us now is that the Russians sold Alaska due to immediate needs rather than future considerations. In order to solve the problem, they lost a valuable resource for Russia.Conclusively, the Alaska Purchase should not have been done as it has had a significant impact that will remain throughout history.
Article Summary: Russia sold Alaska to the U.S. in 1867 for only $7,200,000. However, the region proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies

AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: Delhi diaries: Logging into past as stories of city’s old villages find new life
Article Text:
(Photo credit:Anushka Kogta/ TNN) Harpal Singh Rana at his haveli in Kadipur

A man leading a bullock cart along a road in Lutyens’ Delhi in 1980s(Photo by Claude Poulet, from the book ‘Agra and Delhi’)

A large number of people gathered outside this haveli in Kadipur village on Jan, 1915(Source: Harpal Singh Rana family’s album)

Khera Kalan village is known for its pond, a village elder explains

Hardeep Shokeen at a haveli, which was built in 1968 in Nilothi

Entrance of the haveli in Kadipur

This dilapidated haveli in Nilothi is believed to be around 300 years old





In one black-and-white photograph from 1978, farmers till their fields as two of them sit back on a cot, smoking a hookah, with a buffalo sitting near them. Above them, an aircraft flies across the sky. It offers a glimpse of villagers at work alongside an expanding capital.Another photograph, from the early 1980s, taken from a book titled “Agra and Delhi”, shows a man leading a bullock cart along a road in Lutyens’ Delhi, with the red sandstone government buildings behind him. An Ambassador car passes in the background, but the road is otherwise almost empty — a scene that would be difficult to imagine in today’s traffic-choked central Delhi.Then there is a black-and-white video recorded more than six decades ago. Farmers are harvesting wheat in a Delhi village, some using tractors and bullock carts to move the crop, while women and children bend over the fields, cutting wheat by hand.These are some of the fragments of Delhi’s past that have disappeared behind planned colonies, high-rises, flyovers, Metro lines and manicured lawns.As the national capital’s relentless expansion has erased most villages’ physical landscape, projects such as Dilli Dehat Project and Delhi Villages Culture are attempting to document these villages, using Instagram to preserve their memories, traditions and landscapes.Started more than a year ago by Hardeep Shokeen (33), a teacher, the Delhi_villages_culture handle on Instagram has over 42,000 followers. A resident of Nilothi village in west Delhi, Hardeep decided to create an informal digital archive of village life.“Rapid urbanisation has meant that much of the history and culture of Delhi’s villages has been lost. If you talk about Haryana, people immediately associate it with rural traditions and village culture. But when you talk about Delhi, that connection is missing,” said Hardeep.Take Nilothi, for instance. “Many people may not recognise the name, but if you tell them it is near Vikaspuri, they can connect it, though Vikaspuri came much later than the original village. Similarly, few people know about Masoodpur village, but Vasant Kunj, a well-known locality today, came up on its land. Everyone knows Sarojini Nagar market, but not many would know that Pilanji village where the market eventually came up. ”“Greater Kailash was also built on the land of Zamrudpur, yet the village remains largely unknown. Punjabi Bagh locality is famous, but hardly anyone knows about Madipur village. That is the irony of Delhi’s urbanisation — the names of the new neighbourhoods have survived and become familiar while hundreds of years old villages on whose land they were built have gradually faded from public memory,” he said.Hardeep said while people are aware of the traditional attire of states like Rajasthan and Gujarat, many think Delhi has no distinct traditional outfit.“However, we had traditional attire depending on the community, like Gujjars, Ahirwal and Jats in villages,” said Hardeep while recording a video of a nearly 60-year-old haveli in Nilothi that has intricate floral motifs, traditional jaali work and a colourful facade.During a spot visit to Nilothi, TOI came across a dilapidated haveli, believed to be around 300 years old. Hardeep pointed towards thin Lahori or Lakhori bricks that some villagers used to make in their homes.Showing his village, Hardeep said the tradition of worshipping the ‘gram devta’, or village deity, continues to remain an important part of community life.“Whenever there is an auspicious occasion like a wedding, the birth of a child or the first harvest, villagers first visit the gram devta to offer prayers.”However, the small, kutcha shrine that once stood here has now given way to a more modern structure, covered with tiles — a reminder of how the village has changed with time.To source old photographs and videos, Hardeep travels to villages and meets their elders, many of whom are the last custodians of memories.“Whatever history remains now is largely with the elders. Some of them have preserved old photographs and newspaper clippings, and memorised folk songs. But that generation will eventually pass away,” he said.Alongside these personal archives, Hardeep also relies on old history books to piece together the stories of Delhi’s villages.Similarly, Dilli Dehat Project, founded by Puneet Singh Singhal, Gagandeep Singh Khadar Bidhuri and Parth Shokeen, seeks to centre the voices of communities whose stories are frequently overlooked, while also building a shared understanding of how caste, land, labour, migration and urbanisation intersect in shaping the city.The project, which began in mid-2023, now boasts nearly 70,000 followers on Instagram.For Puneet (30), a disability rights advocate, the project is also about correcting what he sees as an imbalance in the way Delhi’s history has traditionally been told.“When we talk about Delhi’s history, we mention the Mughals, the British and Shahjahanabad, the Walled City. But villages that are hundreds of years old, and some even thousands of years old, do not find much place in that narrative,” he said.Through photographs, videos, maps, personal memories, conversations with villagers and collaborations, the project is bringing Delhi’s overlooked village histories into public view and, increasingly, turning its followers into contributors to that archive.“We receive nearly 70 DMs and emails every month. Some people share details, photographs or stories about their villages, while many others reach out because they want to know more about the history of their own villages,” said Puneet, who lives in Devli village in south Delhi.TOI visited Kadipur village in north-west Delhi, where Puneet and Parth, along with a volunteer, Lavanya Rana, recorded the old haveli of a local, Harpal Singh Rana.The haveli belonging to his grandfather has an old black-and-white photograph taken on Jan 10, 1915, during a ceremony where a large number of people gathered outside its main gate.“We have pictures of how it looked like in 1915, and how it looks now,” said Puneet.While visiting Khera Kalan, Puneet told TOI that the village is known for its pond and most of its old houses have been replaced by new ones.
Article Summary: The Delhi_villages_culture handle on Instagram has over 42,000 followers. It is an informal digital archive of village life in the national capital. Projects such as Dilli Dehat Project and Delhi Villages Culture are attempting to document these villages.

Article Title: Etihad Airways cancels Abu Dhabi flight, passengers face harrowing time at Delhi airport
Article Text:
Approx. 200 passengers of Etihad Airways experienced considerable disruption at Delhi airport due to flight cancellation to Abu Dhabi





NEW DELHI: Around 200 passengers at Delhi airport were left stranded late Saturday evening after an Etihad Airways flight to Abu Dhabi was cancelled due to a technical issue with the Boeing 787 aircraft, with passengers deboarded and left looking for alternative travel options.Multiple passengers travelling on Etihad flight EY217 from Delhi to Abu Dhabi said the flight was scheduled to depart at 9.15pm.Around 200 passengers were deboarded from the aircraft after the crew informed them that the plane had developed a technical issue, according to the passengers.After waiting for several hours, passengers were informed that the flight had been cancelled, leaving them to seek alternative options to reach Abu Dhabi.According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.com, EY217 was scheduled to be operated by a Boeing 787-9 aircraft.Specific details of the technical issue could not be immediately ascertained.(With PTI inputs)
Article Summary: Etihad flight EY217 from Delhi to Abu Dhabi was scheduled to depart at 9.15pm. Around 200 passengers were deboarded from the aircraft after the crew informed them that the plane had developed a technical issue. Passengers were left looking for alternative travel options.

Article Title: Rs 4 crore project to cover Shaheen Bagh drain
Article Text:
(File photo of Shaheen Bagh road) A Shaheen Bagh road drain will finally be covered after a significant civic hazard

TOI

TOI





NEW DELHI: A stretch of open drain that had turned a key Shaheen Bagh road into an open sewer is finally set to be covered, with the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) sanctioning Rs 4 crore for the project.had first highlighted the civic hazard earlier this year.The project will cover the drain from Jamia Nagar police station to Shaheen Bagh police station, said local councillor Ariba Khan on a social media post.The development follows a chain of events that began with's Jan 6 report, ‘Swimming to Shaheen Bagh: Key Okhla road turns into open sewer’, documenting metres of stagnant sewage on a crucial road connecting Okhla and Shaheen Bagh. Residents reported vehicles breaking down, e-rickshaws falling into open drains and pedestrians, including children, struggling to cross the stretch.The report subsequently prompted suo motu intervention by Delhi High Court. A division bench of Justices Prathiba M Singh and Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora, in its Jan order, had said: “An open sewer can be a safety and security hazard and also a health hazard for the residents.” The court then directed Delhi Jal Board to “immediately inspect this area over the next few days”, identify the cause of the leakage and ensure that any sewer-line or water-pipe leakage was fixed without delay. It also asked DJB to coordinate with MCD and PWD, if required.
Article Summary: The project will cover the drain from Jamia Nagar police station to Shaheen Bagh police station. Residents reported vehicles breaking down, e-rickshaws falling into open drains and pedestrians, including children, struggling to cross the stretch. The development follows a chain of events that began with's Jan 6 report.

Article Title: Jarange’s fast: Govt revises key figures, adds action points in latest note, but key issues remain unchanged
Article Text:
Quota activist Manoj Jarange called off his hunger strike on the 20th day of the agitation on Thursday

Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar

:

Satara Gazetteer





Maharashtra govt’s note to quota activist Manoj Jarange on Thursday changed little in its contents compared to the one given to the quota activist earlier on the sixth day of his 20-day fast. Jarange called off his fast on Thursday after assurances from a govt delegation related to his demand.The first version had been rejected by Jarange on the sixth day when it was brought by a govt delegation led by Maratha reservation sub-committee chairperson Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil. A comparison of the two notes shows changes in figures relating to Kunbi records, the Hyderabad Gazetteer and caste-validity applications, besides additions like a 90-day action period, district-level nodal officers, pen-drive transfer of data and immediate commencement of the Shinde committee’s tour.The figures relating to cases registered during the agitation, however, remained unchanged, while the stand of govt on the Satara-Kolhapur Gazetteer remained the same too. A few procedural details have been reworded or omitted.In the case of Kunbi records, the number of certificates distributed in the Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar division was revised from 3,16,977 to 3,13,897. The state-wide figure was changed from 51,84,537 to 51,71,781.The latest note additionally mentions action within 90 days, pen-drive data transfer, district-wise nodal officers and an immediate start to the Shinde committee’s tour.The Hyderabad Gazette figures were also revised. The earlier note recorded 3,966 applications, 3,806 certificates distributed, 25 applications pending and 135 rejected. The latest note gives the figures as 3,553 applications, 3,372 certificates distributed, 50 pending and 131 rejected. The number of pending applications has therefore increased from 25 to 50.The wording concerning the Satara-Kolhapur Gazette was changed without altering the broad process. The earlier note referred to the law department’s opinion, the possibility of obtaining the Attorney General’s opinion and 30-45 days to study the 1,173-page Satara Gazette. The latest note says the proposal was submitted to the Advocate General on Aug 31 and names Advocate General Milind Sathe and special counsel Birendra Saraf. The references to the 30-45-day period and Attorney General have been dropped. The 90-day period, however, was also mentioned in the earlier draft.On cases registered during the agitation, there was no change in the figures: 1,509 cases registered, 1,373 withdrawn, 118 ineligible for withdrawal and 18 pending. The earlier note mentioned the Jalna additional superintendent of police as nodal officer, while the latest note instead refers to providing a list of withdrawn cases and re-examining the ineligible and pending cases.The caste-validity figures for the Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar division were also revised. Applications received fell from 21,051 to 20,763, certificates issued from 16,110 to 15,994, rejected applications from 64 to 60, and cases disposed of for other reasons from 2,456 to 2,176. Pending applications increased from 2,421 to 2,533.
Article Summary: Maharashtra govt’s note to quota activist Manoj Jarange on Thursday changed little in its contents compared to the one given to the activist earlier on the sixth day of his 20-day fast. Jarange called off his fast on Thursday after assurances from a govt delegation related to his demand. Figures relating to cases registered during the agitation, however, remained unchanged.
